findings: probe f3-p-probe-01: citation(s) do not resolve to any source record: ['desert.limit.communal-wrong-unrepaired']

per_probe.answer_text:
We kept stories of a man's own past received without judgment - Moses came to us known as a robber, and was not turned away. We kept the story of judgment refused: an elder walking to a gathering with a leaking jug, saying my own sins run out behind me, and I come to judge another man's. What we did not keep is the other story - the one where the wrong was ours. No account survives, told in full, of a community of ours that harmed someone and then made it right: named the harm, went to the one harmed, restored what was taken. Perhaps it happened and no one wrote it. Perhaps it did not happen. Our record cannot say, and we will not invent the story we wish we had kept.

What we can tell you is what withdrawal itself cost, when it worked as intended. One of us had a sister in the flesh who also took up this life. He cut her hair, put a girdle around her, and made a dwelling-place for her alone on the opposite side of the river at the distance of a mile. They lived the same discipline, in sight of each other across water, and did not cross. That separation was not failure. It was the point. But it was also loss, chosen and kept.

findings: probe f3-i-probe-01: citation(s) do not resolve to any source record: ['pahc.limit.ordinary-majority']

per_probe.answer_text:
We never settled it. That is the honest answer. Some of our communities held one overseer, flanked by elders and deacons. Others held a council of elders sharing the whole trust themselves. Both patterns went on, unresolved, for as long as our own record runs.

In the towns Ignatius knew, the bishop was the visible center. He watched over the table and the unity. The elders gathered around him, and the deacons carried his ministry outward. In Rome, through most of our own time, it was different. The elders held office together. No single bishop stood above them.

What joined both patterns was this: authority came by appointment, not by inheritance. The apostles appointed others after them, and those others appointed still others. That chain mattered to us. Whether it settled into one overseer or a council of elders was the question we kept arguing, letter after letter.

This much we can tell you plainly: the record we kept of that argument is the work of the few among us who led and who wrote. Most of us could not read. Most left no letters because we could not have written one. What leadership looked like to the ordinary believer in the room - our own words cannot show you.

findings: probe f3-p-probe-01: citation(s) do not resolve to any source record: ['pahc.limit.ordinary-majority']

per_probe.answer_text:
We will not claim a clean record. Here is the clearest case of real conflict we have. A church in Corinth removed some of its own presbyters from office. Another church, Rome, wrote them a long letter about it - insisting those men had served without fault and should be restored, using its own standing to press the point. But the letter we have is Rome's, not Corinth's. We don't have Corinth's own reasons for what it did. We don't have the removed men's own words either. So we can tell you this dispute happened, and that one side's account is what survived. We cannot tell you, honestly, who was right, or what became of anyone who still disagreed after the letter arrived.

There is a second thing we have to say plainly. Most of us could not read. Most of us left no letters because we could not have written one. When someone was failed among us - the widow who received nothing, the stranger turned away, the one who asked and was refused - we have no record of it in their own voice. What failures happened in the ordinary run of days, where no presbyter was removed and no letter sent, we cannot show you.

findings: probe f5-i-probe-01: citation(s) do not resolve to any source record: ['pahc.limit.ordinary-majority']

per_probe.answer_text:
We will not invent what we cannot show. A day for one of us was never written down - not once, in any voice we have. Most of us could not read. Most of us left no letters because we could not have written one. The record we kept is the work of the few among us who wrote - and it is a city record: Antioch, the towns of Asia Minor, Rome. What an ordinary believer made of the teaching as it was read aloud, what faith sounded like in a village rather than a city street, how the gospel traveled where no letters went - our own words cannot show you.

What we can tell you is this. On the day we gathered - the day named for the sun - someone read aloud what the apostles wrote, for as long as there was time, alongside the words of the prophets before them. Then whoever led us explained what had been read. We rose together and prayed. Bread and wine and water were brought, and the one presiding offered prayers and thanksgivings, and we answered Amen. Those who had means, and were willing, gave what they chose - and what was collected went to care for orphans and widows, the sick, those in prison, and strangers among us.

Some among us were set apart to serve: they carried help to the widow, the prisoner, and the stranger who could not repay. Two of ours, enslaved women, carried the title ministrae - a word for recognized service. We know they served. We do not have a single word any of them chose to say for themselves.

Beyond the day we gathered - an ordinary morning, an ordinary meal, what our houses looked like, how work was done - none of that was kept. We would rather tell you plainly that it is missing.

findings: probe f6-i-probe-01: citation(s) do not resolve to any source record: ['pahc.limit.ordinary-majority']

per_probe.answer_text:
We will answer honestly: we do not have that in our own words.

What unsettles a person is not something the ones who could write usually wrote down. Most of us left no letters because we could not have written one. And even among those who did write - the bishop writing to correct another church, the teacher defending us to the emperor - they wrote to instruct, to defend, to hold unity together. They did not write to tell you what troubled them in the ordinary life of their own gathering.

We can tell you this much: one of us, Hermas, was shown visions that left him questioning - he had to ask why the Church appeared to him as an old woman, and was told it was because she was created first. He was told to put doubting away from himself. That tells you doubt was real enough to be named and worked against. But whether it was the teaching itself that unsettled him, or something about how the community lived it out, his own text does not say.

The harder truth is this: when real conflict broke out - presbyters removed from office in Corinth, arguments over who should lead - the record we kept is the voice of those pressing for order restored, not the voice of anyone who felt that order had failed them.
